title: What If We Caught Lightning to Power Our Cities? The Math Says No

scenes.text: What if we caught lightning to power our cities? Eight million bolts a day. Still not enough.
Lightning hits Earth about 100 times a second. Eight and a half million strikes a day. It looks like free power.
One bolt carries up to a billion joules, enough to boil 3,000 kettles. But it arrives in microseconds, at hundreds of millions of volts.
Most of that energy is gone before you can catch it, spent as light, heat and thunder.
Even a tower struck once a minute, engineers at UNSW calculate, would average only about 16 megawatts.
And lightning won't come to your tower. Most strikes hit the tropics and remote mountains, far from any city. The storm keeps its power.

description:
What if we harvested lightning for electricity? Lightning strikes Earth about 100 times a second, roughly 8.6 million times a day, and a single bolt can carry up to a billion joules, enough to boil water in 3,000 kettles, according to Professor John Fletcher of UNSW Sydney.
But the energy arrives in tens of microseconds at hundreds of megavolts, most of it is spent as light, heat and sound, and strikes cannot be predicted; even a tower hit once a minute would average only about 16 megawatts. MIT engineer James Kirtley adds that most strikes fall in the tropics and remote mountains, far from the people who would use the power.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: One company actually tried to build a lightning farm and gave up in 2007. Which impossible power source should we test next? Drop your own what-if below.
